Project proposal: Product safety in cross-border e-commerce

Zipiao Wan

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

From: Zipiao Wan (GitHub: Chiver)

Re: Final project proposal: hazards of imported products sold online, and the role of supply-chain reach in foodborne illness

Motivation

Over the last decade a large share of U.S. consumer purchases has moved to online marketplaces (Amazon third-party sellers, Walmart.com Marketplace, Temu, SHEIN, AliExpress, TikTok Shop). Many of these products are manufactured abroad and shipped directly to consumers, often in small parcels that skip the importer and retailer checks used for goods sold in physical stores. Regulators such as the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) have said that this channel is hard to police. This project asks whether that concern shows up in public safety data, and what the data can and cannot tell us about it.

The project has two parts, each with its own dataset and vignette:

  1. Consumer products (main analysis, new dataset): CPSC recall announcements.
  2. Food (class dataset): CDC National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS) outbreaks, provided in this package as waterborne.

Main research question

Among consumer product recalls announced by the U.S. CPSC from 2015 through 2025, are recalls of products manufactured outside the United States and sold only through online channels (exposure) more likely to involve reported injuries or deaths (outcome) than recalls of products sold only in physical stores?

Unit of analysis and population

  • Unit of analysis: one CPSC recall announcement (one recall number).
  • Population: all recalls in the CPSC recall database with a recall date between 2015-01-01 and 2025-12-31. Joint recalls with Health Canada or Mexico’s PROFECO are kept when the U.S. is a recalling jurisdiction. Recalls with no product sold in the U.S. are excluded.

Exposure: sales channel and origin

The exposure is a four-level categorical variable built from the structured fields ManufacturerCountries, Retailers and Importers, and from the free-text “Sold At” statement in each recall notice (for example, “Sold exclusively online at Amazon.com from March 2021 through May 2023”):

Level Definition
Cross-border online-only (exposure of interest) Made outside the U.S. and sold only online (marketplaces or brand websites)
Domestic online-only Made in the U.S. and sold only online
Omnichannel Sold both in physical stores and online
Store-only (reference) Sold only in physical stores

Coding plan:

  • A documented R function, classify_channel(), will apply a dictionary of regular expressions (for example, exclusively online, online at, marketplace domain names, stores nationwide) to the “Sold At” text. The dictionary will be fixed before any outcome tabulation.
  • Validation: I will hand-code a random sample of 100 recalls and report the agreement (sensitivity and specificity) of the automated classification.
  • Missing data: recalls with no manufacturing country get an explicit origin unknown level, and recalls with no channel statement get channel unknown. The primary analysis is complete-case. In a sensitivity analysis the unknown levels are kept as separate categories, to see whether missingness is related to the outcome.

Outcome

  • Primary outcome (binary): whether the recall notice reports at least one injury or death (the Injuries field). “None reported” or “no injuries” is coded 0. Any reported injury, death or incident involving bodily harm is coded 1.
  • Secondary outcomes:
    • the number of reported incidents (a count parsed from the notice text);
    • any reported death (binary and rare, so descriptive only);
    • hazard type (fire/burn, choking, strangulation, laceration, chemical, electrical shock).

Confounders, chosen before looking at the data

  • Product category (children’s products and toys, furniture, household appliances, micromobility and lithium-ion batteries, clothing and textiles, other). Channel mix and injury risk both differ strongly by category.
  • Recall year, which reflects the growth of e-commerce and changes in reporting and enforcement over time, including the COVID-19 period.
  • Number of units recalled (log scale), a proxy for how many consumers were exposed.
  • Intended for children (yes/no), because children’s products fall under stricter rules and injury reports for them may be handled differently.

Hazard type is likely on the causal pathway (for example, imported lithium-ion batteries lead to fire hazards, which lead to burns). For that reason it is not adjusted for in the primary model. It is examined separately as a possible mediator.

Planned analysis

  1. Descriptive statistics: counts and percentages of recalls by exposure level, year, product category, manufacturing country (top 10) and hazard type, plus the median and IQR of units recalled. A time-series plot will show the share of cross-border online-only recalls from 2015 to 2025.
  2. Unadjusted comparison: the proportion of recalls with reported injuries in each exposure level, with 95% confidence intervals.
  3. Adjusted model: logistic regression of the primary outcome on exposure plus the confounders above, reported as adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs. For the incident counts, a negative binomial model with log(units) as an offset.
  4. Sensitivity analyses: treating missing levels as categories; excluding the micromobility/battery category; restricting to 2019-2025.

Second vignette: foodborne outbreaks and supply-chain reach (class dataset)

The second vignette uses the CDC NORS data from class (data(waterborne, package = "finalproject")). It asks a parallel question for food: outbreaks spread across several states usually come from commercially distributed products, often imported produce or packaged foods. These outbreaks are a rough proxy for long, wide supply chains.

Among foodborne outbreaks reported to NORS, are multistate outbreaks (exposure) associated with a higher proportion of ill persons hospitalized (outcome) than single-state outbreaks?

  • Unit and population: one outbreak; all outbreaks whose primary transmission mode is food. NORS flags multistate outbreaks in its location field. I will confirm how that coding works while tidying the data.
  • Exposure: multistate vs. single-state (binary).
  • Outcome: hospitalizations / illnesses per outbreak (a proportion). It will be modeled with a binomial GLM using illnesses as trials, with a quasi-binomial variant for overdispersion. Outbreaks with missing hospitalization information are excluded from the model, and their share is reported by year.
  • Confounders, chosen in advance: etiology (for example, Salmonella, STEC, Listeria, norovirus), outbreak year (decade), and IFSAC food category.
  • Data engineering, following the class stubs:
    • turn the list-structured records into one tidy data frame;
    • convert the year/month fields into Date objects;
    • map states to Census regions using datasets::state.region;
    • compare observed with expected outbreak counts by region and IFSAC category;
    • map the outbreaks with leaflet.
  • Known limitation to discuss: multistate outbreaks are mostly found through laboratory surveillance (PulseNet), which over-samples severe, culture-confirmed cases. Some of any association with hospitalization may therefore come from how outbreaks are detected rather than from the supply chain itself.

Data provenance

Dataset Source Access Status
CPSC recalls U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, Recall Retrieval Web Services (SaferProducts.gov REST API, https://www.saferproducts.gov/RestWebServices/Recall?format=json) Public, no API key; queried by RecallDateStart / RecallDateEnd New, requesting approval
waterborne CDC NORS via Socrata API (https://data.cdc.gov/api/v3/views/5xkq-dg7x/query.json) Included in this package Class dataset

For the CPSC data, a script in inst/scripts/ will download the records, store the retrieval date and query parameters, and save a flattened data frame as data/cpscrecalls.rda. The data will be documented in R/data.R like the other package datasets. The raw JSON will not be changed. All parsing and recoding steps will be written as package functions so they can be re-run when CPSC updates the database.

Planned package deliverables

  • vignettes/proposal.qmd (this document)
  • vignettes/cpsc_crossborder.qmd: provenance, descriptive statistics, models and findings for the main question
  • vignettes/nors_multistate.qmd: tidying, descriptive statistics, models and findings for the food question
  • R functions with roxygen documentation: fetch_cpsc_recalls(), classify_channel(), parse_injuries(), tidy_waterborne()
  • A README summarizing the questions, data and main findings, and the pkgdown site at https://chiver.github.io/finalproject

Expected limitations

  • Recalls are a selected sample. Foreign online sellers often do not cooperate with CPSC, which then issues unilateral warnings instead of recalls. Recall data therefore probably under-represent hazardous cross-border products, so a null result would not mean those products are safe.
  • Injury reports depend on how complaints are collected. These channels differ between marketplaces and physical retailers, so there may be differential outcome misclassification.
  • Exposure comes from text classification. It may be misclassified, which the validation sample is meant to measure.
  • The estimates are associations, not causal effects.

Request to the teaching team

The CPSC recall data are not one of the class datasets, so I am requesting approval to use them for the main vignette. If the teaching team would prefer two class datasets, I will keep the NORS vignette and replace the CPSC analysis with an analysis of cdcfiremort together with gunleg. I would also welcome feedback on whether the four-level exposure definition is too fine-grained for the expected sample size.
